# Spec template

The structure every SPEC.md follows in this project. Adapted from the artstudio template for a build run as a Factory Mission: milestones instead of team phases, one mission branch, one pull request.

```text
# <product> — Spec for the mission
Owner: David Carbajosa (architect, reviewer, the human in lane 7). Implementers: one Factory Mission (orchestrator, workers, validators) under ai/RULES.md. Status: v<X.Y> (<date>). Living document: §9 is the human feedback channel, §10 the as-built history.

## 1. Purpose            what it is, for whom, what it must prove, what is out of scope (explicitly); the PRD it implements and the review notes it answers
## 2. Mission setup      the mission command with its flags (models per role, reasoning effort, output format), the mission branch name, the worktree policy, the gate command, the hooks that must be active, the usage budget per milestone, what the human will and will not answer mid-mission
## 3. Milestones         Walking skeleton first (core crate, canonical event, replay of one capture, empty board). Then one milestone per PRD section in the order the PRD gives: for each, the tests it turns green, its acceptance commands, its gate, its exit criterion, what it must not touch. M0 freezes the stream mapping before later milestones are planned in detail. A milestone is integrated into the mission branch, never shipped
## 4. Versions           table: component, version, source, verified date (crates, Tauri, toolchain, images, actions)
## 5. Architecture       crates and their interfaces, the canonical event and lane mapping (versioned), the store schema, the ingest adapters behind traits, config keys with defaults, metric definitions by reference to the PRD, runtime limits, security (keychain, read-only raw lines, the one outward write)
## 6. Tests              per suite: what it covers, where it runs (local / mission branch CI / final PR), the command; fixtures are captured streams, named and dated
## 7. CI                 jobs on the mission branch (light, under three minutes warm) and on the final pull request (full, attested); what each gates; required checks
## 8. Deliverables       README contents, docs/decisions/ (one file per decision, generated index), BACKLOG.md, build-log/ (hook logs), ai/session/ (session log with transcript links), reports/ (usage and waste per milestone, pasted from the tool)
## 9. Changelog and human feedback   | Id | Date | Feedback | Applies | Status |   (written by the orchestrator on the mission branch, never in a worktree)
## 10. Evolution log     one row per integrated milestone: what landed, tests green, usage spent, deviations, unknown events left   (written at integration, from the workers' and validators' reports)
```

Each decision in §5 carries a one-line reason. Numbers come from the PRD unless the spec says why they changed. The spec is written by a Droid in an interactive spec session (PRD, review notes, RULES.md and this template as inputs) and approved by the human before the mission starts; the mission plans from the approved spec, it does not write it.

## RULES
# Rules

The rules this project inherits, adapted for a build run as a Factory Mission (orchestrator, workers, validators) with the human as owner. Derived from the artstudio set (14-oct-2026); rules that only made sense for a hand-run team are struck, not deleted, so the decision is visible.

1. **Tests before code.** No production code without a failing test that asks for it. Workers write the test first and commit it red; validators check that the red run exists in the log. Tests are the contract between the spec and the build.
2. **A walking skeleton first.** The thinnest end-to-end slice (core crate, canonical event model, `observatory replay` over one captured session, an empty board that starts) is on the mission branch before any milestone deepens its area, so every integration is checked by real acceptance tests.
3. **Versions verified, latest stable.** Every crate, tool and image is pinned to a version checked against the official source on the day it is added; the spec's version table says when.
4. **No secrets, no magic values.** Credentials only from the OS keychain or the environment, never in the repo, the store or the logs; every number (poll interval, stall threshold, price) comes from configuration with a stated default and a reason in the spec.
5. **Everything from a clean clone.** `cargo test`, `cargo run -p observatory-cli -- replay <fixture>` and the app build work on a machine that has only the Rust toolchain and the Tauri prerequisites; the README's commands are the ones CI runs.
6. **CI is a gate, not infrastructure.** Light checks on the mission branch: `cargo fmt --check`, `clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test`, the replay fixtures, `cargo deny` (advisories and licences), gitleaks. The full attested run on the one pull request into `main`: everything above plus Semgrep (SAST), Trivy filesystem scan on `Cargo.lock`, Checkov on the workflows themselves, an SBOM (`syft` or `cargo-sbom`), the Tauri bundle built on macOS, build provenance with `actions/attest-build-provenance`, cosign-signed artifacts, with the Trivy results and the SBOM attached to the release. It never deploys.
7. **Counts come off the tool.** Test counts, timings, token usage and scan results are pasted from the run that produced them, never estimated.
8. **The spec is as-built.** When the code and the spec disagree at the end of a milestone, the spec is updated in the same integration, with the reason in `docs/decisions/`.
9. **Deviations are the human's to approve.** The orchestrator proposes, with reason and cost, and waits.
10. **Honest time.** The README states the real time and usage spent per milestone; what was left out is listed, not hidden.
11. **CI under three minutes warm on the mission branch.** Independent jobs in parallel, cargo and tool caches, prebuilt actions; the heavy stage only on the final pull request. Measured per run and reported.
12. **Git forward only, one PR per mission.** Never amend, reset, rebase or stash; a mistake is fixed by a new commit. Milestones live in worktrees and are integrated into `mission/<name>`; nothing reaches `main` except the mission's single pull request. A milestone is never shippable; the mission is.
13. **One file per decision, no shared files across worktrees.** `docs/decisions/D-NNN-slug.md` (what, why, alternatives, consequences); the index is generated. Two worktrees never edit the same file; the living spec sections are written by the orchestrator on the mission branch at integration time.
14. **Review fixes what blocks.** Blocking and security findings are fixed in the milestone, once; everything else goes to `BACKLOG.md` with its reason. A review never starts a second round for style.
15. **Nothing reaches an agent mid-task.** Decisions are settled before a milestone starts; what comes up later waits for the next milestone or goes to the backlog. The human messages the mission only at milestone boundaries or when the stall flag is up.
16. **Deliverables grow with the work.** README, decisions, backlog, build-log and the session log start with the skeleton and are extended at every integration, never written at the end.
17. **Everything is logged.** Hooks record every tool call to `build-log/`; every session transcript is linked from the session log; usage per model and per milestone is recorded. The build of the observatory is itself a dataset for the observatory.
18. **Unknown is surfaced, never dropped.** An event the mapper does not recognise is counted and shown; a milestone that adds a source ends with zero unknown events on its capture.
19. **Models per role are declared.** Orchestrator, worker and validator models are named in the spec and in the mission command; a change of model is a decision file.

Struck from the artstudio set: *tester, coder and reviewer as separate agents per team* (the Mission's workers and validators take those roles; if the validators prove weaker, custom sub-droids bring the split back, as a decision); *the 90-minute box* (replaced by usage budgets per milestone).

## 1. Summary

droid-observatory is a Rust desktop application that shows how a Factory Mission moves through the engineering build cycle. It renders the mission as a board whose lanes are the orchestrated states of a mission, from the human's intent through orchestration, building, validation, integration, the human gate, and the outside ecosystem (PR, CI, deploy). Alongside the flow it measures what the flow costs: cycle time, waste by cause, tokens and money per sub-droid and per model.

The observatory attaches to missions started from any terminal on this machine (it watches `~/.factory/sessions/` and tails each new session file as it grows), replays finished ones from the same files, and can also host a mission itself (it spawns `droid exec --mission` and consumes the JSON-RPC event stream, which adds the control channel). Attach is the primary live mode; hosting is the secondary path. It never copies the event data into a second source of truth: every lane entry is a view over the raw JSONL line it came from.

A mission is not complete when the workers stop. It is complete when the gate is green and the merge has happened.

## 2. Delivery model

This section defines the units the board shows. Everything else follows from it.

- **A mission is a business feature: the unit that ships.** For this project, v1 of the observatory. A mission ends in **one PR into `main`**, outcome-sized, with the evidence attached. The full attested CI runs on that PR; CD runs from `main`.
- **Milestones are internal iterations**, not shippable. Each milestone runs in its own worktree and is integrated into a **`mission/<name>` branch**, the mission's interface to `main`. Fast checks (tests, lint, the gate command) run on that branch to keep it healthy. Nothing on it is shippable or pretends to be.
- **The mission branch is short-lived by construction.** It dies at the merge. That is what keeps it from becoming a long-lived `dev` branch.
- **Features** are the orchestrator's work items inside a milestone. Workers build them, validators judge them, and metrics are computed at feature granularity, then rolled up to the milestone and the mission.
- **The fix loop after CI red reopens the mission on its branch.** It does not open a new PR. The same PR goes green or stays red.

On the board: **cards are milestones**; the gate group in lane 8 is the mission's one PR; lane 6 is integration into `mission/<name>`; lane 8 is the PR.

**Models per role** (decision D-006; `ai/RULES.md` rule 19): orchestrator `claude-fable-5-1`, workers `claude-sonnet-5-5`, validators `claude-opus-5-5`. Reasoning effort per role is declared in the spec. A change of model is a decision file.

## 3. Problem

Mission Control (CLI and Factory App) shows progress, workers, and a log. It does not show:

- the mission's full life, including what happens after the workers stop (PR, CI, attestations, deploy, red builds that need a fix);
- where time goes: active work versus waiting on a human, waiting on validation, waiting on merge, rework after a blocking finding, retries and conflicts;
- what each role and model consumed, so that model and reasoning-effort choices can be compared with real numbers;
- a single place to act when the mission needs a human: approve, answer, redirect, merge.

Running missions without that view means managing agents blind on the two dimensions that matter most for an engineering organization: flow and cost.

## 4. Goals

1. Show every milestone of a mission across the nine lanes defined in section 7, live and in replay, with features visible inside each card.
2. Show per card: validation state (red/green), current agent, gate state, and a Details view with review notes, validation criteria, commits, and raw event links.
3. Let the human act from the board: pause/resume the orchestrator, send instructions, answer escalations, approve, mark a feature complete or skipped, and merge the PR when policy says a human merges.
4. Measure cycle time, waste by cause, mission overhead, and bottlenecks per feature, per milestone, per role, and per mission.
5. Measure cost: tokens per sub-droid, converted to Factory Standard Credits when the stream exposes them, otherwise money via a dated price table that every displayed cost references.
6. Treat CI red on the mission PR as a counted rework loop: reopen the mission on its branch, loop the affected card back into the Workers lane, keep the same PR.

## 5. Non-goals (v1)

- Replacing Mission Control for planning. The observatory starts after a plan exists (it may launch the mission, but the plan conversation stays in Droid).
- Multi-user or server deployment. v1 is a single-user desktop app reading local data and the user's own GitHub access.
- Writing to Factory's hosted API beyond what the local `droid` process already does.
- Editing code or reviewing diffs inside the app. It links out to the worktree, commit, or PR.
- Supporting CI systems other than GitHub Actions in v1 (adapter boundary is defined so others can follow).

## 6. Users

**Mission owner (primary).** The engineer acting as project manager of agents. Wants to see progress, act when needed, and know what the mission cost in time and money.

**Reviewer / gatekeeper.** Opens the Details view, reads scrutiny findings and QA results, watches the outcome video, and merges or sends back.

**Engineering lead (reader).** Compares missions and models over time: cycle time, waste, cost per feature. Does not intervene.

## 7. Lanes

The board has nine lanes. Lanes 1–6 are fed by the mission stream, 7–8 by GitHub and human actions, 9 by session metadata. Each event carries `session_id`, `role`, `model`, `timestamp`, `duration`, and a pointer to its raw JSONL line.

## 8. Board model

**Card = one milestone.** The milestone is the spec phase: the orchestrator plans it, workers build its features in a worktree, validators judge it, and it integrates into `mission/<name>`. Each card lists its features with their individual state, and metrics roll up feature → milestone → mission.

A card moves left to right. Its position is the lane where its most recent open activity is. The Details view shows the full history across lanes.

**Gate group.** Lane 8 holds one group per mission: the mission PR. All cards of the mission share that gate state; the badge sits on the group. Until the PR exists, lane 8 shows the mission branch with its fast-check status as a pre-gate placeholder.

**Fix loop.** When CI goes red on the mission PR, the observatory reopens the mission on `mission/<name>` with a cycle tagged `fix` on the milestone(s) whose features the fix touches. Those cards are drawn with a loop arrow back into lane 3. The PR stays the same. The loop is counted as rework in lane 9.

**Mission completion.** Mission state is `complete` only when the PR is merged with CI green. Until then it is `planning`, `building`, `validating`, `at gate`, or `fixing`.

- **Branch badge** (card): fast checks on `mission/<name>` passed / failed / running for this milestone's integration.
- **Gate badge** (group): `pending` (no PR), `checks running`, `review requested`, `human required`, `ruleset blocked`, `policy-merged`, `CI green`, `CI red`.

Opened via the Details button on a card. Tabs:

- FR-D1 **Timeline**: every event for the milestone and its features across all lanes, each with role, model, duration, and a link that opens the raw JSONL line.
- FR-D2 **Review notes**: scrutiny findings (blocking / non-blocking, status: open / resolved), user-testing scenario results with evidence (screenshots, video).

All actions are logged as lane 7 events with the human as actor.

- FR-H3: Answer an open question or approve/deny a permission request raised by any sub-droid.

- FR-H5: Stall detection: a feature with no active time for a configurable threshold is flagged; the flag suggests the matching troubleshooting prompt (frozen mission, stuck worker, repeated failure).

### 9.6 Metrics (FR-M)

Definitions in section 10. All metrics are available per feature, per milestone, per role, per model, and per mission, and exportable as CSV/JSON.

- FR-M1: Cycle time per feature, per milestone, per mission, and per lane.
- FR-M2: Waste by cause, including waiting on merge and mission overhead reported separately.
- FR-M3: Bottlenecks: lanes and roles with the longest queue time and highest WIP; queued-behind-WIP idle is a bottleneck signal, unscheduled idle is not.

### 9.7 Mission lifecycle (FR-L)

- FR-L1: Attach (primary live mode): watch `~/.factory/sessions/` with a filesystem notifier, detect any new session JSONL (a mission started from any terminal on this machine), tail it as it grows and render it within 1 s, named by its `--tag` or session id. No control channel.

The app spawns `droid exec --mission --input-format stream-jsonrpc --output-format stream-jsonrpc`; this is the only mode with a control channel (pause, message, answer).

## 10. Metric definitions

### 10.1 Time states

Each feature, at every instant, is in exactly one time state:

| State | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Active** | A worker, validator, or orchestrator is doing something for the feature: tool call in flight or model generating. |
| **Waiting on human** | A question or approval is open and nobody is acting (lane 7 open, lanes 2–6 idle for this feature). Sub-causes: *question*, *permission*, *waiting on merge* (checks green, policy requires a human, nobody has merged). |
| **Waiting on validation** | Work is done, validator not started. |
| **Retry and failure** | Time in tool errors, `hook.blocked`, re-runs of the same command, and conflict resolution. |
| **Idle, queued** | Feature is planned and ready but blocked behind another feature (WIP limit, dependency, no free worker). A bottleneck signal. |
| **Idle, unscheduled** | Feature exists but nothing is scheduled and nothing is blocking it. Not a bottleneck signal. |

Rework is not a separate time state. It is a window (10.2) that overlays active, retry, and waiting time.

### 10.2 Rework windows

A **rework window** opens at a blocking signal and closes at its resolution event, per signal:

| Opens | Closes |
|---|---|
| `finding.blocking` | `rework.resolved` |
| `qa.scenario.failed` | `qa.scenario.passed` for the same scenario |
| `integration.conflict` | `integration.conflict_resolved` |
| `check.failed` (mission PR) | `check.passed` for the same check |

Overlapping windows on the same feature merge into one. A window with no closing event stays open until mission end and is reported as unresolved.

- **Rework time** = active time inside rework windows.
- **First-pass active time** = active time outside any rework window.

This bounds rework so that legitimate new work after a fix is not counted as waste.

### 10.3 Mission overhead

Orchestrator time before the first `feature.defined`, replanning time not attributable to one feature, and `context.compacted` recovery belong to no card. They are reported as **mission overhead**, a separate line in lane 9, never apportioned silently. An optional explicit apportionment (equal split across features) can be switched on for comparisons and is labeled as such.

### 10.4 Derived measures

- **Cycle time** (feature) = `feature.defined` → feature's last `task.done` with validation green and integrated. **Cycle time** (milestone) = `milestone.defined` → `milestone.completed`. **Cycle time** (mission) = `intent.created` → `pr.merged` (human or policy) with CI green. Stage cycle times are computed per lane.
- **Waste** = total elapsed − first-pass active time, split by cause: waiting on human (question, permission, merge), waiting on validation, rework, retry and failure, idle queued, idle unscheduled. Mission overhead is reported next to waste, not inside it. Reported per feature, per milestone, and per role.
- **Bottleneck** = lane or role with the highest sum of waiting plus queued time across features in the window, and the lane with the highest WIP relative to its throughput.
- **Fix loops** = count of `fix` cycles per milestone and per mission.

### 10.5 Cost

- Token counts are taken from `usage.reported` events per session (input, output, cache read, cache write when available).
- If the stream reports Factory Standard Credits, credits are the primary unit.
- Otherwise cost = Σ tokens × price per model and token class, from the **price table**: a dated config file (`~/.droid-observatory/prices/<YYYY-MM-DD>.toml`). The board always shows the date of the table it used, and a mission keeps the table it started with unless the user re-prices it explicitly.
- Cost is shown next to waste so that a slow, cheap model and a fast, expensive one can be compared on the same panel.

## 11. Data sources and architecture

### 11.1 Sources

| Source | Mode | Provides |
|---|---|---|
| `~/.factory/sessions/<cwd-slug>/<session-id>.jsonl` (+ `.settings.json`), watched | **Attach (primary live mode)** | The observatory watches `~/.factory/sessions/` with a filesystem notifier, detects any new session JSONL (a mission started from any terminal on this machine), tails it as it grows and renders it in real time, named by its `--tag` or session id. Worker and validator events via the child session files. These are the canonical raw lines that lane entries link to. Read-only: no control channel. |
| Same files, finished | Replay | Same adapter: replay is attach at end-of-file, plus the time scrubber. |
| `droid exec --mission --input-format stream-jsonrpc --output-format stream-jsonrpc` | Host (secondary live mode) | Every orchestrator event; token usage; permission and question requests; the control channel (pause, message, answer). Started from the app's launch screen. |
| Git (local) | Live, polled | Mission branch, milestone worktrees, integration commits, fast-check results. |
| GitHub REST/GraphQL (user token) | Live, polled | The mission PR, reviews, check runs, required checks, rulesets, attestations, merges, deploy statuses. |
| App actions | Live | Lane 7 human events. |

Attach is primary because missions are started from the terminal in practice; the launch screen is the secondary path. Hosting is the only mode with a control channel; attach and replay are read-only views over the same files.

Open items: the exact JSON-RPC event schema for missions (how worker child sessions, feature ids, milestone ids, and validator roles are identified) is not fully documented, and where `--tag` is recorded (session settings file or first stream line) is unconfirmed. M0 captures a real mission stream, confirms both, and freezes the mapping from raw events to lane events as a versioned module with fixtures.

### 11.2 Components

```text
┌─────────────────────────── Tauri 2 shell ───────────────────────────┐
│  UI (webview)                                                        │
│   board · details · agents · metrics · launch · settings            │
└──────────────▲───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │ Tauri commands + events (serde types shared with core)
┌──────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ observatory-core (Rust lib)                                          │
│  ingest/   jsonl_watch · jsonl_tail (attach; replay = attach at EOF) │
│            droid_rpc (host) · git · github                           │
│  model/    Event · Feature · Milestone · Agent · Lane mapping        │
│            (versioned by Droid version)                              │
│  metrics/  time states · rework windows · overhead · cycle · waste · │
│            bottleneck · cost                                         │
│  store/    SQLite index: events(ptr→jsonl file,offset), features,    │
│            milestones, agents, pr, checks, prices                    │
│  control/  pause · message · answer · mark · merge                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **The lane is a view, not a copy.** The store indexes events with a pointer to the raw JSONL line (file, byte offset). Opening an event in the UI reads the raw line on demand.
- `observatory-core` has no UI dependency and is testable from fixtures (recorded mission streams). A thin CLI (`observatory replay <session>`) exercises it headlessly and is the first thing that works.
- The GitHub adapter is behind a trait so other forges and CI systems can follow.

### 11.3 Security

- GitHub token and Factory credentials stay in the OS keychain (Tauri keyring plugin). Never written to the store or logs.
- Raw JSONL may contain secrets from tool output; the app renders it read-only and never uploads it.
- Merge is the only outward-facing write. It requires an explicit confirmation naming the PR and target branch.

### 11.4 Telemetry export (Grafana Cloud)

Two kinds of telemetry leave the app, both over OpenTelemetry OTLP (`http/protobuf`) to a Grafana Cloud stack, both off by default so the app works fully offline (decision D-004):

- **App telemetry**: `tracing` spans for ingest, mapping, metrics, and control; errors as span events.
- **Mission metrics**: the lane-9 series, so the budget meter and waste can be charted and alerted on outside the desktop window. Metric names are a contract: `observatory.mission.cycle_seconds`, `observatory.feature.cycle_seconds`, `observatory.waste_seconds`, `observatory.rework_windows`, `observatory.fix_loops`, `observatory.tokens.{input,output,cache_read,cache_write}`, `observatory.cost_usd`, `observatory.unknown_events`.

Contract (owner, D-010): OTLP over HTTP to `https://otlp-gateway-prod-eu-west-2.grafana.net/otlp` (`/v1/metrics`, `/v1/traces`, `/v1/logs`). The `Authorization=Basic …` header value is read at runtime from the macOS keychain item with service `droid-observatory/otlp-headers` and account = current user; never written to config, the store or logs; if the item is missing, telemetry stays off and the UI says so. Resource attributes: `service.name=droid-observatory`, `service.version`. Metric labels only from `mission`, `milestone`, `role`, `model`, `cause`; never session id, event id or free text. Counters and histograms only, no per-event gauges. The spec states the number of active series the app adds and keeps it under 200 (B-017). Config keys and defaults: `config/observatory.example.toml` `[telemetry]`. CI telemetry is deferred (B-002).

## 12. Technology options and recommendation

Constraint: Rust. Preference: Tauri 2. Needs: data-dense board, live updates, charts, markdown and video rendering in Details, long-lived subprocess management, SQLite.

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Tauri 2 + Leptos (Rust, CSR via Trunk)** | Single language; shared serde types between core and UI with no bindings; fine-grained reactivity suits a live board; webview gives markdown, video, CSS layout for free. | Charting ecosystem thinner than JS; WASM/Trunk toolchain adds build steps; smaller community. **Droids have far less Leptos in their training than React or Svelte**, so worker rework on UI tasks is likely higher. **The WASM/Trunk toolchain inside a Mission is a new failure mode** (toolchain install, target, dev server) that validators may struggle to diagnose. |
| B. Tauri 2 + Dioxus | Same single-language benefit; React-like ergonomics; growing fast. | Dioxus also ships its own desktop renderer, which blurs the "why Tauri" story; same training-data and toolchain concerns as A. |
| C. Tauri 2 + TypeScript (Svelte or React) | Richest charting and UI libraries; fastest to a polished UI; best-known stack for Droids. | Two languages; types must be generated (ts-rs/specta) and kept in sync; the user's stated preference is Rust. |
| D. iced (native) | Pure Rust, no webview, small binary, Elm architecture fits an event-driven board. | Markdown, video, and rich text are weak; complex layouts cost more effort; no Tauri plugin ecosystem (keyring, updater, tray). |
| E. egui (native, immediate mode) | Trivial live updates and plots (egui_plot); excellent for dashboards. | Looks like a tool, not an app; text-heavy Details view (review notes, markdown) is awkward; accessibility and theming limited. |

**Recommendation: Option A, Tauri 2 + Leptos, with M1 as an explicit go/no-go.**

Reasoning: the hard part of this product is `observatory-core` (ingest, mapping, metrics), not the UI. Keeping the UI in Rust means the metric types, lane mapping, and event model are used directly in the view with no translation layer, which is where drift and bugs would otherwise appear. The webview covers the rich-content needs (markdown findings, QA video, PR rendering) that native options handle poorly. Charting is the one real gap; lane 9 needs stacked bars and timelines, achievable as SVG from Leptos signals, with a JS chart library as a documented escape hatch.

**Go/no-go criterion (evaluated at M1 completion):** the board renders the M0 replay (all nine lanes, cards positioned correctly, Details timeline open) with **at most 3 worker sessions of rework** after the first scrutiny pass, and the Trunk/WASM build succeeds from a clean checkout with the documented command. If either fails, switch to Option C for M2 onward, keeping `observatory-core` unchanged; the Tauri command boundary is designed to make that swap possible. (Threshold of 3 agreed 2026-10-22; may be adjusted at planning time.)

## 14. Risks and open questions

| Risk / question | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Mission JSON-RPC event schema is not fully documented; mapping to features, milestones, and validator roles may be heuristic. | M0 captures and freezes a versioned mapping with fixtures; `unknown.event` is counted and shown, never dropped; M0 is the gate before detailed planning. |
| Leptos: less Droid training data than React/Svelte; WASM/Trunk toolchain is a new failure mode inside a mission. | Core first and headless; M1 go/no-go with a written criterion; swap to TypeScript at the Tauri command boundary. |
| Factory Standard Credits may not be exposed per session in the stream. | Price table fallback is first-class; the UI always names the unit and the price-table date. |
| Attestation formats vary (GitHub artifact attestations, SLSA provenance, custom). | v1 reads GitHub artifact attestations and check-run conclusions (`attestation.recorded`), verifies via GitHub's attestation API where possible (`attestation.verified`); others appear as opaque recorded events with a link. |
| Merge policy lives in several places (branch protection, rulesets, CODEOWNERS, org policy). | v1 reads branch protection and rulesets, plus an explicit app-level override per repo; the Details gate tab shows which rule decided. |
| A `fix` cycle after the orchestrator has ended needs a follow-up mission with the right context on the same branch. | The fix launch pre-fills the mission file with the feature spec, the failing check output, the mission branch, and the original session ids. |
| Local JSONL files may change format between Droid versions. | The mapper is versioned by the Droid version observed in the session settings file; replay of old captures stays in the test suite. |
| Filesystem notifiers coalesce or miss events (macOS FSEvents latency, a session file created before the watcher starts). | The watcher is paired with a poll at `[ingest].jsonl_poll_ms`; on start the sessions directory is scanned and files already growing are attached; attach latency is measured in M1 acceptance, not assumed. |
| `--tag` may not be recoverable from the session files. | M0 confirms where it is recorded; if absent, sessions are named by id and the first `mission.started` payload. |
| M4 cannot be tested on the observatory repo itself. | Private demo repository with PR flow, CI, and rulesets, prepared before M4. |
| M5 has no oracle unless a human produces one. | Reference spreadsheet from the M0 capture is a listed mission input. |
| Webview charting in Rust is thinner than JS. | Scoped chart set (stacked bars, timeline, sparkline) built as SVG components; JS chart lib as a documented escape hatch. |

## 15. Acceptance criteria for this PRD

The PRD is accepted when the reviewer agrees that:

1. The delivery model (mission = shippable business feature, milestones = internal iterations on `mission/<name>`, one PR) is stated correctly.
2. The nine lanes, their sources, and their event kinds are correct and complete, with `unknown.event` as a first-class kind.
3. Card = milestone, features inside the card, one gate group per mission PR, and the fix loop reopening the mission on its branch match the intended workflow.
4. The time states, bounded rework windows, first-pass definition, mission overhead, waiting on merge, and the queued/unscheduled idle split are the ones to measure against.
5. Attach as the primary live mode, replay from the same files, hosting as the secondary path with the control channel, plus git and GitHub adapters is the right v1 data source set.
6. The stack recommendation (Tauri 2 + Leptos) with the M1 go/no-go criterion is approved, or a different option is chosen.
7. The milestone plan (M0 as planning gate, demo repo for M4, human reference for M5) is acceptable as the seed of the mission plan.

## Appendix A: Canonical event

```rust
pub struct Event {
    pub id: EventId,
    pub mission_id: MissionId,
    pub milestone_id: Option<MilestoneId>,
    pub feature_id: Option<FeatureId>,
    pub lane: Lane,                 // Intent | Orchestrator | Workers | Scrutiny | UserTesting | Integration | Human | Outside
    pub kind: EventKind,            // every kind in section 7, plus Unknown { raw_type: String }
    pub role: Role,                 // Orchestrator | Worker | ScrutinyValidator | UserTestingValidator | Human | External
    pub session_id: Option<SessionId>,
    pub model: Option<ModelId>,
    pub at: Timestamp,
    pub duration: Option<Duration>,
    pub usage: Option<TokenUsage>,  // input, output, cache_read, cache_write, credits
    pub source: SourcePtr,          // Jsonl { path, byte_offset } | Git { repo, sha } | GitHub { url } | App
}

pub struct ReworkWindow {
    pub feature_id: FeatureId,
    pub opened_by: EventId,         // blocking signal
    pub closed_by: Option<EventId>, // resolution event; None = unresolved at mission end
    pub cause: ReworkCause,         // Scrutiny | UserTesting | Integration | Gate
}
```

## Appendix B: Glossary

- **Mission**: a business feature, the unit that ships. One PR into `main`.
- **Mission branch**: `mission/<name>`, the mission's interface to `main`. Short-lived; dies at the merge.
- **Milestone**: an internal iteration inside a mission; runs in its own worktree; integrates into the mission branch; one card.
- **Feature**: the orchestrator's work item inside a milestone; the granularity at which metrics are computed.
- **Sub-droid**: any agent session spawned for the mission: orchestrator, worker, scrutiny validator, user-testing validator.
- **Integration**: landing a milestone worktree on the mission branch, with fast checks. Not a merge in the gate sense.
- **Gate**: the mission PR into `main`, merged by a human or by policy, triggering attested CI and possibly CD.
- **Fix cycle**: a mission cycle tagged `fix` on the affected milestone(s) after CI red at the gate. Same branch, same PR.
- **Rework window**: the span from a blocking signal to its resolution on one feature.
- **First-pass active time**: active time outside any rework window.
- **Mission overhead**: orchestrator time attributable to no feature; reported separately.
- **Waste**: elapsed time that is not first-pass active time, split by cause.

## Entry 4 — Final design decisions before PRD draft

**Decisions (user, via questionnaire)**

**Lanes (exact, ordered):**

1. **Intent**: mission prompt, spec, acceptance criteria; later human re-prompts. Few events.
2. **Orchestrator**: plan, feature breakdown, milestones, task assignment, replans.
3. **Workers**: one sub-lane per worker (or per feature when the mission names them); events: task started, files touched, tests run, commits, task done.
4. **Validators, scrutiny**: review findings, blocking vs non-blocking, re-work requested.
5. **Validators, user testing**: QA runs against the built thing, scenario results.
6. **Integration**: worktree merges into the mission branch, conflicts, gate command runs ("integrated in mission", not "merged").
7. **Human**: approvals, answers to escalations, review of the outcome (the video), the merge of the PR.
8. **Outside**: GitHub PR opened, CI runs and attestations, deploys (ecosystem lane; empty for the observatory itself).
9. **Time, Waste, Cost and models**: tokens and usage per role, which model did what; doubles as budget meter; elapsed time, time stuck/wasted.

Every event carries session id, role, model, timestamp, duration, and a link to the raw JSONL line. **The lane is a view, not a copy.** Lanes 1–6 from the stream, 7–8 from GitHub and human actions, 9 from session metadata.

**Waste definition (user):**
- Active time: worker/validator/orchestrator doing something (tool call in flight, model generating).
- Waiting on human: question/approval open, nobody acting (lane 7 open, lanes 2–6 idle).
- Waiting on validation: work done, validator not started.
- Rework: time spent after a blocking finding on the same task.
- Retry and failure: tool errors, re-runs of same command, integration conflicts.
- **Waste = everything that is not active time on first-pass work**, split by cause, per feature and per role. Cost shown next to it (tokens × per-model multiplier) so slow-cheap vs fast-expensive models compare honestly.

**Gate (lane 8 + badge):** final lane holds the gate (PR opened → checks → merged); card badge shows gate state (pending, human required, policy-merged, CI green/red). **CI red reopens the mission**: new mission cycle on the same feature tagged `fix`, drawn as a loop back into Workers lane. Merge button appears only when policy says a human merges; otherwise badge flips to policy-merged automatically. A mission is complete when the gate is green and the merge happened, not when workers stop. Every red is a counted rework loop in lane 9.

**Card:** one card = one mission feature. Gate lane groups cards by the PR that carries them, badge on the group. A PR with three features shows three cards sharing one gate state. CI red loops back only to the card the fix touches.

**Cost:** tokens + Factory Standard Credits if the stream exposes them, else a price table. **Price table lives in a dated config file so every cost on the board names the prices it used.**

## docs/decisions/D-010-telemetry-contract.md
1→# D-010: Telemetry contract for the Grafana Cloud stack
2→
3→**Date:** 2026-10-22
4→**Status:** accepted (owner-provided contract; code in the telemetry milestone)
5→
6→## Context
7→
8→D-004 chose Grafana Cloud over OTLP and sketched metric names with a wide attribute list
9→(`feature`, `session`, `class`, `unit`, `price_table`, a gauge for active agents). The owner
10→has provisioned the stack and set the operating constraints below. Cardinality on Grafana
11→Cloud is billed per active series, so the attribute set is the contract that matters.
12→
13→## Decision
14→
15→- **Transport:** OTLP over HTTP (`http/protobuf`) to
16→  `https://otlp-gateway-prod-eu-west-2.grafana.net/otlp` (`/v1/metrics`, `/v1/traces`,
17→  `/v1/logs`). The endpoint is not a secret and lives in `config/observatory.example.toml`.
18→- **Credential:** the full `Authorization=Basic …` header value is read at runtime from the
19→  macOS keychain item with service `droid-observatory/otlp-headers` and account = the
20→  current user. It is never written to config, the store or logs. If the item is missing,
21→  telemetry stays off and the UI says so (a visible "telemetry: off, no keychain item"
22→  state, not a silent failure). The environment variable `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` is
23→  for CI only (B-002); the app does not read it.
24→- **Resource attributes:** `service.name=droid-observatory` and `service.version` (the
25→  crate version). Nothing else. D-004's `deployment.environment` and `service.namespace`
26→  are dropped.
27→- **Metric attributes (labels):** only from the set `mission`, `milestone`, `role`,
28→  `model`, `cause`. Never a session id, event id, feature id or free text. Anything
29→  that varied by `class`, `unit` or `status` in D-004 becomes part of the metric name
30→  (for example `observatory.tokens.input`, `observatory.cost_usd`) or is not exported.
31→- **Instruments:** counters and histograms only. No per-event gauges;
32→  `observatory.active_agents` is not exported (it stays an in-app view).
33→- **Series budget:** the spec states the exact metric set and the number of active series
34→  the app adds, computed from the label cardinalities, and keeps it **under 200**. The
35→  arithmetic is the spec's (B-017); the shape it must fit is: one mission exporting at a
36→  time, up to 6 milestones, 3 roles, up to 4 models, a closed list of waste causes, and a
37→  histogram costs one series per bucket plus `_sum` and `_count`, so explicit bucket
38→  boundaries are part of the contract.
39→
40→## Alternatives
41→
42→- Keep D-004's attribute list and rely on Grafana's adaptive metrics to aggregate: pays for
43→  the series first, then hides them; rejected.
44→- Export per-feature series: `feature` would be the largest cardinality by far and is
45→  already visible in the app; rejected by the owner.
46→- Read the header from the environment as a fallback in the app: one more place a secret can
47→  leak into a shell history or a log; rejected by the owner.
48→
49→## Consequences
50→
51→- D-004 stays accepted for the choice of backend and the two kinds of telemetry; its
52→  attribute list, resource attributes and the gauge are superseded here.
53→- `config/observatory.example.toml` `[telemetry]` carries the endpoint, the keychain
54→  service name, the allowed label set, the series budget and the revised metric names.
55→- PRD v0.5 §11.4 states the contract. `.env.example` marks the OTLP variables CI-only.
56→- B-017: the spec session computes the series count and names the histogram buckets.

# D-006: Models per role for the mission

**Date:** 2026-10-22
**Status:** accepted

## Context

Rule 19: orchestrator, worker and validator models are declared in the spec and the
mission command; a change is a decision file. The owner set the roles on 2026-10-22.

## Decision

| Role | Model |
|---|---|
| Orchestrator | `claude-fable-5-1` |
| Workers | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| Validators (scrutiny and user testing) | `claude-opus-5-5` |

Declared in `.factory/settings.json` (`missionOrchestratorModel`,
`missionModelSettings.workerModel`, `missionModelSettings.validationWorkerModel`), the
README mission command, `config/observatory.example.toml` `[mission]`, and the price table
`config/prices/2026-10-22.toml`. Reasoning effort per role is set in `SPEC.md` §2.

## Alternatives

Same model for all roles (simpler, loses the cost/quality split the observatory is meant
to measure); cheaper validators (validation is where correctness is bought).

## Consequences

Lane 9 compares roles across these three models from the first mission. Changing any of
them: new decision file, update the four places above.

\# Missions Configuration & Reference

Configuration inheritance, headless execution with droid exec --mission, mission settings, and enterprise access policy.

\## Configuration inheritance

Missions inherit your existing Droid configuration:

{/\\* sweep-allow: term-bullets \*/}

\- \*\*MCP integrations\*\*: Workers can use your connected tools (Linear, Sentry, Notion, etc.)
\- \*\*Custom skills\*\*: Your existing skills are available and new ones can be developed during planning.
\- \*\*Hooks\*\*: Lifecycle hooks fire during mission execution.
\- \*\*Custom droids\*\*: Subagents configured in your project are available to workers.
\- \*\*AGENTS.md\*\*: Workers follow your project conventions and coding standards.

\## Headless mission execution

Missions can also run non-interactively via \`droid exec --mission\`. This is useful for CI, scheduled jobs, and any environment where you want the orchestrator to plan and execute without a live TUI.

\`\`\`bash
droid exec --mission -f mission.md
\`\`\`

You can override the models and reasoning effort used by the orchestrator's worker and validator agents:

\`\`\`bash
droid exec --mission \
 --worker-model claude-sonnet-4-6 \
 --worker-reasoning-effort medium \
 --validator-model claude-opus-4-7 \
 --validator-reasoning-effort high \
 -f mission.md
\`\`\`

\| Flag \| Description \|
\| \-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\- \| \-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\- \|
\| \`--mission\` \| Run \`droid exec\` in Mission Mode (multi-agent orchestration). \|
\| \`--worker-model \` \| Model used for mission worker agents. \|
\| \`--worker-reasoning-effort \` \| Reasoning effort for mission worker agents. \|
\| \`--validator-model \` \| Model used for mission validator agents. \|
\| \`--validator-reasoning-effort \` \| Reasoning effort for mission validator agents. \|

See \[\`droid exec\`\](/droid-exec/overview) for the full headless reference.

\## Configuration

Missions are tuned through the \`missionModelSettings\` object and a few top-level keys. Set these in your user or project \[settings\](/droid-cli/settings) file. Organization administrators can also provide model and reasoning defaults through \[Enterprise Controls\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control#mission-defaults).

\| Setting \| Description \|
\| \-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\- \| \-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\-\- \|
\| \`missionModelSettings.workerModel\` \| Default model used by mission worker subagents. \|
\| \`missionModelSettings.workerReasoningEffort\` \| Reasoning effort for mission workers. Options are model-dependent (see \[/models\](/models)). \|
\| \`missionModelSettings.validationWorkerModel\` \| Model used by validation workers (scrutiny and user-testing). \|
\| \`missionModelSettings.validationWorkerReasoningEffort\` \| Reasoning effort for validation workers. \|
\| \`missionModelSettings.skipScrutiny\` \| Skip scrutiny validation milestones during missions. \|
\| \`missionModelSettings.skipUserTesting\` \| Skip user-testing validation milestones during missions. \|
\| \`missionOrchestratorModel\` \| Model used by the mission orchestrator. \|
\| \`missionOrchestratorReasoningEffort\` \| Reasoning effort for the mission orchestrator. \|
\| \`keepSystemAwakeDuringMissions\` \| Prevent the OS from sleeping while a mission is running. Defaults to \`true\`. \|

The six mission model and reasoning fields resolve independently with \[session-default precedence\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control#how-precedence-works-hard-controls-vs-session-defaults). Org-managed values act as fallbacks for more-local settings. \`skipScrutiny\` and \`skipUserTesting\` remain user-managed and are not accepted in org-managed settings.

 Pairing a strong orchestrator model with a faster worker model is a common cost-quality tradeoff: planning and validation benefit most from extra reasoning, while routine worker tasks can use a lighter model.

\## Enterprise: restricting mission access

Organizations can restrict who is allowed to launch missions through the \`missionPolicy\` org-level setting:

\`\`\`json
{
 "missionPolicy": {
 "restrictedAccess": true,
 "allowedUserIds": \["user\_123", "user\_456"\]
 }
}
\`\`\`

When \`restrictedAccess\` is \`true\`, only members listed in \`allowedUserIds\` can start new missions. See the \[settings reference\](/droid-cli/settings) for the full enterprise policy surface.

 Run missions non-interactively with \`droid exec --mission\`.

 Govern mission access and model policy at the organization level.

\# Running in the Factory App

Use Factory Missions in the Factory App to plan and execute large, multi-feature projects with structured orchestration.

!\[Mission Control dashboard in the Factory App\](/docs-assets/images/mission-web.webp)

\## The Mission Control dashboard

While you can run Missions from the CLI, the Factory App provides a rich, visual Mission Control dashboard. This interface helps you act as a project manager by giving you greater visibility into what your orchestrator, workers, and validators are doing.

\## Starting and resuming Missions

{/\\* sweep-allow: term-bullets \*/}

\- \*\*Start a new mission:\*\* Start a new session in \*\*Mission Mode\*\*, or start a mission directly from the Mission Control page. Start the Mission before doing the work you want it to plan and orchestrate; do not use a long-running normal session as a substitute and convert it afterward.
\- \*\*Continue a past mission:\*\* Navigate to the [Mission Control tab](https://app.factory.ai/missions) to find past missions, review their current state, and resume execution exactly where you left off.
\- \*\*Run on remote machines:\*\* When starting a mission, you can select a \*\*Droid Computer\*\* as your target environment. This allows long-running missions to execute safely in the background on persistent remote machines without tying up your local workspace.

\## Navigating the UI

The Mission Control dashboard gives you real-time visibility into your multi-agent workflows:

{/\\* sweep-allow: term-bullets \*/}

\- \*\*Track Progress:\*\* See exactly what has been done so far. The top bar tracks overall time and credits, while the right sidebar maintains a live progress log of every worker and milestone.
\- \*\*Select Models:\*\* Use the model dropdowns in the right sidebar to configure different models for the Orchestrator, Worker, and Validator agents on the fly.
\- \*\*Inspect Features:\*\* The main view provides a high-level summary of the active milestone. You can drill down into any feature to review its specific validation criteria and commits.
\- \*\*Examine Workers:\*\* The left sidebar lists all active and completed workers. Select a specific worker to view its detailed terminal output, thought process, and any sub-tasks it completed.
\- \*\*Intervene & Redirect:\*\* If a Mission appears stuck or priorities change, pause the orchestrator directly from the UI, instruct it to re-assess or re-plan, and then resume execution.

\# App settings

Manage personal session defaults and organization usage alerts in the Factory App.

The Factory App lets you set personal session defaults so every new session starts the way you want. Your choices are \*\*capped by org policy\*\*: if your organization enforces hard controls, your preferences take effect only within the boundaries those controls allow. See \[Enterprise Controls & Managed Settings\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control) for the org side.

\## Session defaults

Session defaults are applied when a new session starts. In the Factory App, use the mode selector for \*\*Normal Mode\*\*, \*\*Spec Mode\*\*, or \*\*Mission Mode\*\*, and the Autonomy selector for \`Auto Off\`, \`Auto Low\`, \`Auto Medium\`, or \`Auto High\`.

\### Default model

Set \`model\` to a \[model ID from the catalog\](/models). This is the model new sessions use unless you pick a different one from the model selector. For custom models, see \[Custom Models (BYOK)\](/model-independence/byok).

\### Reasoning effort

\`reasoningEffort\` adjusts how much structured thinking the model performs before replying. The available levels and the default are \*\*set by each model\*\*, so the \[Available Models\](/models) table is the source of truth for what a given model accepts. Across the catalog they range from least to most deliberation:

{/\\* sweep-allow: term-bullets \*/}

\- \*\*\`off\` / \`none\`\*\*: no structured reasoning (fastest).
\- \*\*\`minimal\`\*\*, \*\*\`low\`\*\*, \*\*\`medium\`\*\*, \*\*\`high\`\*\*: progressively more deliberation.
\- \*\*\`extra high\`\*\*, \*\*\`max\`\*\*: the deepest reasoning, where a model offers it.

\### Interaction mode

\`sessionDefaultSettings.interactionMode\` sets whether new sessions start in \*\*Normal Mode\*\* (\`auto\`) or \*\*Spec Mode\*\* (\`spec\`). In the app, the mode selector switches between the two. See \[Interaction Modes\](/autonomy-and-safety/specification-mode) for what each mode does.

\### Autonomy level

\`sessionDefaultSettings.autonomyLevel\` sets the default \[Autonomy Level\](/autonomy-and-safety/auto-run) for new sessions: \`off\` keeps manual approvals; \`low\`, \`medium\`, and \`high\` pre-authorize work at or below that risk level. In the app, the Autonomy selector chooses \`Auto Off\`, \`Auto Low\`, \`Auto Medium\`, or \`Auto High\`.

\### Spec mode overrides

When sessions start in Spec Mode, you can use a different model and reasoning effort for planning:

\- \`sessionDefaultSettings.specModeModel\`: the model used for spec mode planning. See \[Models\](/models) for available IDs.
\- \`sessionDefaultSettings.specModeReasoningEffort\`: reasoning effort for the spec mode model. Same values as \`reasoningEffort\`.

\### Delegation defaults

If your organization uses \[Delegations\](/delegations), you can set a personal model, reasoning level, and custom instructions under \*\*Settings → Session Defaults → Delegations\*\*. These apply only to work you delegate from Slack, Linear, or Jira: your model and reasoning level override the organization's defaults when policy allows, and your instructions are added to the organization's instructions. These defaults are saved to your Factory account, not \`settings.json\`. See \[Set personal delegation defaults\](/delegations#set-personal-delegation-defaults).

\## Cloud session sync

When \`cloudSessionSync\` is on, sessions are mirrored to the Factory App so you can revisit conversations from any browser. Your organization can control whether cloud sync is enabled at the org level; see \[Enterprise Controls & Managed Settings\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control).

\## Organization usage alerts

Open \*\*Settings → Usage → Organization Usage\*\* to view your active organization's Standard FSC usage for the current calendar month. The month follows the billing subscription's time zone. Usage is scoped to the active organization, not rolled up across every organization in the enterprise.

 This section is available to Enterprise organizations with organization usage alerts enabled. All organization members can view usage. Only Owners and Managers can change the threshold or email setting.

\### Set a monthly alert threshold

1\. Select \*\*Set threshold\*\*.
2\. Enter a positive amount in \*\*Monthly Alert Threshold (M credits)\*\*. For example, \`50\` means 50 million credits.
3\. Select \*\*Save\*\*.

The usage display shows credits consumed, the saved threshold, and the percentage used. Without a threshold, it shows \*\*Unlimited\*\*. Select \*\*Edit threshold\*\* to change the amount, or \*\*Remove threshold\*\* to clear it.

 The monthly alert threshold is informational, not a real-time usage limit. Reaching it never blocks usage or changes billing. It does not replace individual credit caps or your contracted billing terms.

\### Enable organization alert emails

After saving a threshold, turn on \*\*Organization Usage Alert Emails\*\*. Emails are off by default and notify the organization's active Owners and Managers at 80% and 100% of the threshold.

Turn the switch off to stop emails while keeping the threshold visible. Removing the threshold also disables emails; setting a new threshold does not automatically turn them back on. These controls are stored for the organization in the Factory App, not in personal \`settings.json\`.

Changes to the threshold or email setting appear in the \[audit log\](/enterprise/audit-log#organization-usage-alert-settings).

\## How your preferences interact with org policy

Your personal defaults are \*\*session defaults\*\*, not hard controls. They use the most-local-wins precedence: your choice overrides an org default, and a runtime override (such as a \`--settings\` flag or an in-app selector change) overrides your saved default. But org hard controls always cap what you can choose:

\- \`modelPolicy\` (\`allowedModelIds\`, \`blockedModelIds\`) decides which models exist at all. You can pick any allowed model, but blocked models are not available.
\- \`maxAutonomyLevel\` caps the effective \`autonomyLevel\` no matter who set it. If the org sets \`medium\`, your \`high\` default is clamped to \`medium\`.

In short: your org decides the \*\*boundaries\*\*, and you pick your \*\*preferred defaults inside those boundaries\*\*. For the full hierarchy, merge semantics, and org schema, see \[Enterprise Controls & Managed Settings\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control).

{"title":"https://docs.factory.com/factory-app/settings.md","status":200,"markdown":"\\# App settings\n\nManage personal session defaults and organization usage alerts in the Factory App.\n\nThe Factory App lets you set personal session defaults so every new session starts the way you want. See \\[Enterprise Controls & Managed Settings\\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control) for the org side.\n\n\\## Session defaults\n\nSession defaults are applied when a new session starts. In the Factory App, use the mode selector for \\*\\*Normal Mode\\*\\*, \\*\\*Spec Mode\\*\\*, or \\*\\*Mission Mode\\*\\*, and the Autonomy selector for \\`Auto Off\\`, \\`Auto Low\\`, \\`Auto Medium\\`, or \\`Auto High\\`.\n\n\\### Default model\n\nSet \\`model\\` to a \\[model ID from the catalog\\](/models). This is the model new sessions use unless you pick a different one from the model selector. For custom models, see \\[Custom Models (BYOK)\\](/model-independence/byok).\n\n\\### Reasoning effort\n\n\\`reasoningEffort\\` adjusts how much structured thinking the model performs before replying. The available levels and the default are \\*\\*set by each model\\*\\*, so the \\[Available Models\\](/models) table is the source of truth for what a given model accepts. Across the catalog they range from least to most deliberation:\n\n{/\\\\* sweep-allow: term-bullets \\*/}\n\n\\- \\*\\*\\`off\\` / \\`none\\`\\*\\*: no structured reasoning (fastest).\n\\- \\*\\*\\`minimal\\`\\*\\*, \\*\\*\\`low\\`\\*\\*, \\*\\*\\`medium\\`\\*\\*, \\*\\*\\`high\\`\\*\\*: progressively more deliberation.\n\\- \\*\\*\\`extra high\\`\\*\\*, \\*\\*\\`max\\`\\*\\*: the deepest reasoning, where a model offers it.\n\n\\### Interaction mode\n\n\\`sessionDefaultSettings.interactionMode\\` sets whether new sessions start in \\*\\*Normal Mode\\*\\* (\\`auto\\`) or \\*\\*Spec Mode\\*\\* (\\`spec\\`). In the app, the mode selector switches between the two. See \\[Interaction Modes\\](/autonomy-and-safety/specification-mode) for what each mode does.\n\n\\### Autonomy level\n\n\\`sessionDefaultSettings.autonomyLevel\\` sets the default \\[Autonomy Level\\](/autonomy-and-safety/auto-run) for new sessions: \\`off\\` keeps manual approvals; \\`low\\`, \\`medium\\`, and \\`high\\` pre-authorize work at or below that risk level. In the app, the Autonomy selector chooses \\`Auto Off\\`, \\`Auto Low\\`, \\`Auto Medium\\`, or \\`Auto High\\`.\n\n\\### Spec mode overrides\n\nWhen sessions start in Spec Mode, you can use a different model and reasoning effort for planning:\n\n\\- \\`sessionDefaultSettings.specModeModel\\`: the model used for spec mode planning. See \\[Models\\](/models) for available IDs.\n\\- \\`sessionDefaultSettings.specModeReasoningEffort\\`: reasoning effort for the spec mode model. Same values as \\`reasoningEffort\\`.\n\n\\### Delegation defaults\n\nIf your organization uses \\[Delegations\\](/delegations), you can set a personal model, reasoning level, and custom instructions under \\*\\*Settings → Session Defaults → Delegations\\*\\*. These apply only to work you delegate from Slack, Linear, or Jira: your model and reasoning level override the organization's defaults when policy allows, and your instructions are added to the organization's instructions. These defaults are saved to your Factory account, not \\`settings.json\\`. See \\[Set personal delegation defaults\\](/delegations#set-personal-delegation-defaults).\n\n\\## Cloud session sync\n\nWhen \\`cloudSessionSync\\` is on, sessions are mirrored to the Factory App so you can revisit conversations from any browser. Your organization can control whether cloud sync is enabled at the org level; see \\[Enterprise Controls & Managed Settings\\](/enterprise/hierarchical-settings-and-org-control).\n\n\\## Organization usage alerts\n\nOpen \\*\\*Settings → Usage → Organization Usage\\*\\* to view your active organization's Standard FSC usage for the current calendar month. The month follows the billing subscription's time zone. Usage is scoped to the active organization, not rolled up across every organization in the enterprise.\n\n This section is available to Enterprise organizations with organization usage alerts enabled. All organization members can view usage. Only Owners and Managers can change the threshold or email setting.\n\n\\### Set a monthly alert threshold\n\n1\\. Select \\*\\*Set threshold\\*\\*.\n2\\. Enter a positive amount in \\*\\*Monthly Alert Threshold (M credits)\\*\\*. For example, \\`50\\` means 50 million credits.\n3\\. Select \\*\\*Save\\*\\*.\n\nThe usage display shows credits consumed, the saved threshold, and the percentage used. Without a threshold, it shows \\*\\*Unlimited\\*\\*. Select \\*\\*Edit threshold\\*\\* to change the amount, or \\*\\*Remove threshold\\*\\* to clear it.\n\n The monthly alert threshold is informational, not a real-time usage limit. Reaching it never blocks usage or changes billing. It does not replace individual credit caps or your contracted billing terms.\n\n\\### Enable organization alert emails\n\nAfter saving a threshold, turn on \\*\\*Organization Usage Alert Emails\\*\\*. Emails are off by default and notify the organization's active Owners and Managers at 80% and 100% of the threshold.\n\nTurn the switch off to stop emails while keeping the threshold visible. Removing the threshold also disables emails; setting a new threshold does not automatically turn them back on. These controls are stored for the organization in the Factory App, not in personal \\`settings.json\\`.\n\nChanges to the threshold or email setting appear in the \\[audit log\\](/enterprise/audit-log#organization-usage-alert-settings).\n\n\\## How your preferences interact with org policy\n\nYour personal defaults are \\*\\*session defaults\\*\\*, not hard controls. They use the most-local-wins precedence: your choice overrides an org default, and a runtime override (such as a \\`--settings\\` flag or an in-app selector change) overrides your saved default. <coding_guidelines>
# AGENTS.md

How agents work in this repository. The rules are in [ai/RULES.md](ai/RULES.md) and win over
anything here; this file is the operational summary.

## What this is

droid-observatory: a Tauri 2 + Leptos (Rust) desktop app that shows a Factory Mission moving
through nine lanes, with validation, gate, agent attribution, waste and cost per sub-droid.
PRD: `ai/prd/droid-observatory-prd.md`. Spec (when written): `SPEC.md`.

Current state: no application code. The walking skeleton (core crate, canonical `Event`,
`observatory replay` over one captured session, an empty board that starts) is the first
thing the mission lands, before any milestone deepens its area.

## Setup, build, test

```sh
make doctor          # tool check with install hints
make hooks           # enable .githooks (once)
make check           # all light checks = mission-branch CI
make fmt             # rustfmt (no-op until Cargo.toml exists)
make lint            # clippy -D warnings
make test            # cargo test --workspace
make deny            # cargo-deny advisories, licences, bans
make replay-fixtures # observatory-cli replay over fixtures/streams/*.jsonl
make app-dev         # Tauri dev window (after the app exists)
```

Toolchain: `rust-toolchain.toml` (1.99.1, rustfmt, clippy, wasm32 target). Do not change it
without a decision file.

## Interactive QA path

Until the app exists: `make check` is the only runnable target.
Once the skeleton lands, the path the validators follow is:

1. `make doctor` reports no missing required tools.
2. `cargo run -p observatory-cli -- replay fixtures/streams/<capture>.jsonl` prints lane
   events and ends with `unknown events: 0`.
3. `make app-dev` opens the window; open the same fixture (Replay); the nine lanes render
   and a card opens its Details view.
4. With the window open, start `droid exec --mission ...` in a terminal; the new session
   appears on the board (Attach) and each event shows within 1 s.

No login gate: the app watches and reads local session files and uses the GitHub token from the keychain or
`GITHUB_TOKEN` only for the gate lane.

## Layout and ownership

```text
crates/observatory-core   ingest, model, metrics, store, control (no UI deps)
crates/observatory-cli    headless replay/inspect over core
apps/observatory-app      Tauri 2 shell + Leptos UI
fixtures/streams          captured mission streams, named <YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.jsonl
docs/decisions            D-NNN-slug.md, one per decision; README.md is generated
docs/runbooks             recovery procedures: red gate, fix cycle, stall, hooks, release
reports/                  usage, waste, readiness; pasted from tools
build-log/                tool-call log written by .factory hooks
ai/                       PRD, rules, template, session logs
```

Crate and app paths are the contract the Makefile and CI probe for; keep them.

## Conventions

- Rust 2024 edition, `rustfmt.toml` and `clippy.toml` as committed. Warnings are errors.
- Naming: standard Rust (`snake_case` items and modules, `CamelCase` types, `SCREAMING_SNAKE`
  consts). Event kinds mirror the PRD §7 names in `snake_case`
  (`finding.blocking` → `FindingBlocking`). Lane and role enums use the PRD's words.
- Tests: unit tests in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` next to the code; integration tests in
  `crates/<crate>/tests/<topic>.rs`; fixture-driven tests read `fixtures/streams/`. Test
  functions read as sentences: `rework_window_closes_on_resolution()`.
- Tests before code (rule 1): commit the red test, then the code that turns it green.
- No magic numbers: every threshold lives in `config/observatory.example.toml` with a reason.
- Debt markers: `TODO(#123)` or `TODO(B-123)`; anything else fails `make check-todos`.
- Markdown: `.markdownlint-cli2.yaml`; links must resolve (`make check-links`).
- Files over 200 KB fail CI unless under `fixtures/streams/` or `build-log/`.

## Git

- Forward only (rule 12): never amend, reset, rebase, stash, or force-push. Fix with a new
  commit. `.factory/hooks/guard-git.sh` and `.githooks/pre-push` enforce this.
- Nothing reaches `main` except the mission's single pull request. `main` has a ruleset:
  PR required, `gate` check required, no force push, no bypass.
- Milestones live in worktrees and integrate into `mission/<name>`. Two worktrees never edit
  the same file (rule 13); shared files (`SPEC.md` §9–10, `README.md`, `BACKLOG.md`,
  `docs/decisions/README.md`) are written by the orchestrator at integration time.
- Commit subject under 72 characters; co-author trailer for agent commits:
  `Co-authored-by: factory-droid[bot] <138933559+factory-droid[bot]@users.noreply.github.com>`.

## Decisions, backlog, logs

- A decision is one file: `docs/decisions/D-NNN-slug.md` with `**Date:**`, `**Status:**`,
  context, decision, alternatives, consequences. Run `make decisions-index` after adding one.
- Deferred work goes to `BACKLOG.md` as `B-NNN` with a reason, not into TODOs or issues.
- Every session is logged under `ai/session/` with transcript links; every tool call is
  logged to `build-log/` by the PostToolUse hook. Do not disable the hooks.
- Usage and waste per milestone go to `reports/` pasted from the tool that produced them.

## Mission setup

Models per role (rule 19; `.factory/settings.json`; D-006):

| Role | Model |
|---|---|
| Orchestrator | `claude-fable-5.1` |
| Workers | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| Validators (scrutiny, user testing) | `claude-opus-5-5` |

Command: see README "Running it as a mission". Reasoning effort per role is set in `SPEC.md`.
A model change is a decision file.

The human answers only at milestone boundaries or when the stall flag is up (rule 15).
Deviations from the spec are proposed with reason and cost, and wait for approval (rule 9).

## Environment and secrets

See `.env.example`. Secrets come from the OS keychain (`droid-observatory/<name>` entries)
or the environment, never from the repository, the store, or logs. Raw session JSONL may
contain secrets: render read-only, never upload, never copy into the store.

Grafana Cloud OTLP (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*`) is the telemetry backend; export is off unless
`[telemetry].enabled = true`.
